title: Why do businesses struggle finding reliable contract manufacturers for small batches?
summary: New brands need 200 units to test a product, but factories quote minimums of thousands. Here's "BatchMatch", a small-batch sourcing assistant a small team could build with Claude in a weekend.
who: Founders of new consumer brands (apparel, personal care, home goods, snacks) and small businesses that want a private-label or custom product made in a first run of a few hundred units. They do not know which factories take small orders, they get ignored when they ask, and a wrong pick costs them their launch capital.
facts: **Legacy minimums are far above a test batch.** ZYOD's co-founder told Inc42 that most apparel manufacturers had set minimum orders at about 2,000 pieces per style, with traditional cycles of 120 to 180 days ([Inc42](https://inc42.com/?p=519053)).

**Packaging often sets the real minimum.** A D2C playbook notes that a factory able to run 200 units can be blocked by a 1,000-unit box minimum, and suggests generic packaging with a branded sticker for pilots ([eChai Ventures](https://echai.ventures/d2c/d2c-find-manufacturers-india/negotiate-moq-small-batch)).

**Smaller first orders cost more per unit.** The same playbook puts the premium for halving a first order at roughly 10 to 15% per unit, and calls it usually the right trade while validating ([eChai Ventures](https://echai.ventures/d2c/d2c-find-manufacturers-india/negotiate-moq-small-batch)).

**Small orders get deprioritised.** A sourcing platform's own blog says high minimums force brands to overproduce and that low-volume orders are frequently pushed back in the queue ([factori](https://blog.factori.com/2025/12/31/low-moq-manufacturing-factori-co)).

**The squeeze is getting tighter in 2026.** Inc42 reports manufacturers asking D2C brands for cash-and-carry terms instead of the earlier 45 to 60 day credit, with several citing a 15 to 20% rise in overall costs ([Inc42](https://inc42.com/features/why-indias-d2c-brigade-is-facing-its-toughest-test-yet/)).
players: Managed manufacturing platforms are growing. ZYOD reports $21.5 million raised and says it serves 550+ D2C companies and can lower minimums on request ([Inc42](https://inc42.com/?p=519053)). Lal10 runs a "cloud factory" over 50+ partner factories with low minimums and a 35-day cycle ([YourStory](https://yourstory.com/2025/06/lal10-cloud-factory-indian-apparel-revolution)). factori aggregates demand across brands to make small runs viable ([factori](https://blog.factori.com/2025/12/31/low-moq-manufacturing-factori-co)). These mostly take on production themselves; we found little that helps a founder screen, compare and brief independent factories on their own.
pitch: "BatchMatch" turns a product idea and a target quantity into a shortlist of factories likely to accept it, a clear request-for-quote, and a side-by-side comparison of the replies.
features: A short guided chat turns a founder's idea into a factory-ready brief: materials, sizes, packaging, quantity, target price and deadline.
Matches the brief against a curated database of factories tagged by category, city, stated minimum order and past small-batch work.
Sends the brief by email or WhatsApp in the factory's preferred language and tracks who replied.
Reads replies, including PDFs and photos of handwritten quotes, and lines up unit price, minimum, packaging minimum, lead time and payment terms.
Drafts a counter-offer using known levers: a paid sample run, generic packaging, a slightly higher unit price for a smaller first order.
capabilities: Builds the web app, the factory database, outreach integrations and tests.
Writes the brief, translates outreach, extracts terms from messy quotes and drafts negotiations.
A "small-batch sourcing" skill holds category checklists and negotiation levers so every brief and counter-offer follows the same rules.
A clickable quote-comparison table to show founders before writing any backend.
Gmail and Google Sheets connectors to send briefs and keep the shortlist in a sheet the founder already uses.
A daily follow-up on factories that have not replied, and a weekly digest of new quotes.
plan: Choose one category (for example apparel or cosmetics) and list 30 factories from trade directories and referrals, with stated minimums.
Ask Claude for an artifact of the brief and the comparison table. Show it to three first-time founders.
Write the sourcing skill: checklist per category, red flags, and five negotiation levers.
Use the starter prompt in Claude Code to build the brief flow, factory table and matching.
Add quote upload and extraction; test on ten real quotes, including a photographed one.
Connect email sending and a reply tracker; add the daily follow-up as a scheduled task.
Deploy, onboard two founders, and run one real request-for-quote end to end.
prompt:
Build a Next.js + TypeScript + Postgres web app called "BatchMatch" for Indian founders sourcing small manufacturing runs (100-1,000 units).

Flow: founder answers a guided chat -> Claude API produces a structured brief (category, materials, sizes, packaging, quantity, target unit price, deadline) as JSON
-> app matches the brief against a factories table (category, city, stated MOQ, packaging MOQ, small-batch history, contact, language) and returns a ranked shortlist with reasons
-> founder approves; app emails each factory a request for quote in their language and tracks replies
-> founder uploads quotes (PDF or photo); Claude extracts unit price, MOQ, packaging MOQ, lead time, payment terms, sample cost into a comparison table
-> 'Draft counter-offer' uses rules from /skills/small-batch-sourcing.md (paid sample run, generic packaging, smaller first order at higher unit price).

Include seed data for 20 sample factories, unit tests for matching and extraction, and a README. Keep the email provider behind an interface in /lib/outreach.ts.
pricing: Free: one brief and a shortlist of five factories.
Rs 1,999 per sourcing project, or Rs 2,999 a month for unlimited briefs and quote comparison.
Later: a listing fee or success fee from factories that want small-batch leads.
risk: Factories may not reply to an automated request from an unknown brand, so the shortlist is only as good as the factory data and relationships behind it.
test: Before building, send 40 hand-written briefs (made with Claude) to factories in one category and city. Count replies and usable quotes within a week. A reasonable bar: at least 12 replies and 6 quotes at or under 500 units.
caution: Present factory details as unverified until checked, get consent before storing contact data, and remind founders to sign a basic non-disclosure and quality agreement before sharing designs.
sources: Inc42: How ZYOD is powering on-demand fashion manufacturing
eChai Ventures: Negotiating MOQ for a small batch
Inc42: Why India's D2C brigade is facing its toughest test yet
take: Founders I meet rarely fail for lack of a product idea; they stall at the first factory call. The useful part of this build is the brief and the comparison: AI turning a vague idea into something a factory owner takes seriously, and five messy quotes into one clear choice.
